rv.q: In all the design elements, this gutsy new "Porgy" has the glimmer of the ideal solution to forging a show that would honor original intentions, keep Sondheim happy and yet reinvigorate this problematic but masterful piece of theater for a new generation.
Ms. McDonald’s Bess is — in a word — great; the show in which she appears is, at best, just pretty good.
This "Porgy Lite" is not nearly as electrifying as the real thing.
At the same time, there’s little to get excited about: “The Gershwins’ Porgy and Bess,” as it’s now titled, is perfectly adequate — but this Theater production won’t take your breath away.
The delight in this production is that it seems to move along swiftly as something both new and old - taken on its own terms, as fresh as it is genuine.

"The Gershwins' Porgy and Bess," which trims the show's length to two and a half hours and adds new dialogue by avant-garde playwright Suzan Lori-Parks, both preserves the integrity of the original piece and makes for absolutely thrilling musical theater.
In the end, though, this is an approachable and heartfelt version of Porgy and Bess that showcases George Gershwin's glorious melodies and the bottomless talents of McDonald.
Performances are strong and they have a wonderful ensemble cast.

Now that the far-from-happy dust has settled from Stephen Sondheim’s preemptive broadside, now that the Theater production of “The Gershwins’ Porgy and Bess’’ has finally arrived on Broadway, it can be seen, and gloriously heard, for what it is: a fully realized work that pays homage to a classic while infusing it with new, thrilling life.
The Gershwins‘ opera adapted by Susan-Lori Parks and directed by Diane Paulus as a Broadway musical is charming, vivid, delightful and moving.

cn.t: This streamlined revival divides critics, though most agree Audra McDonald delivers a mesmerizing performance. The production earns praise for beautiful singing and staging, but some find the controversial revisions timid or unnecessary.

sg.ra: Krapp's stadium-style orchestra kicks in at Row L, so the rake elevates you above the flat front rows while keeping you ahead of the Mezzanine overhang line (Row M). AVFMS reviewer groovybones: 'Row M (and 1 row before/all after) are elevated from the lower ORC, didn't have to crane my neck or worry about tall people'; lynnep: 'recommend row L, great elevation.' SeatPlan calls Rows L-M 'unobstructed head-on views' with enhanced elevation — the rare spot that gets close-and-level without the craning of A-E or the overhang risk of S-X.

The Front Mezz hangs forward over the orchestra (SeatPlan: 'hangs a bit too far forward over the stage') which is a liability for some shows but a feature for Hamilton specifically — AVFMS reviewer anonymous (Nov 2025): 'Close enough to see all facial expressions... but also able to see and appreciate all the choreography since you're above.' The direct overhead angle is called out by TickPick and SeatPlan as 'perfect for taking in large set pieces and choreography' — a Richard-Rodgers-specific reframe where the forward hang becomes the choreography-viewing advantage.

Rear Mezz Row A is a Richard-Rodgers quirk worth knowing — AVFMS anonymous (Jan 2026): 'the front row of the rear Mezz (Row G) is separated from the front Mezz and is raised up a few feet. In front of you is a curtain and you can extend your feet/legs far more than a traditional seat.' SeatPlan confirms 'a curtain rather than a solid wall' gives Row A 'some of the best legroom in the theater,' unusual in a house otherwise notorious for 5-inch knee clearance. Cheapest tier, genuinely unobstructed thanks to the cantilevered single balcony (Wikipedia: balcony 'cantilevered over orchestra to reduce obstructed views').

The Mezzanine overhang begins at Row M but becomes aggressive after Row S per SeatPlan: 'patrons may need to duck slightly to see elevated stage action, particularly in rows W and X.' This matters at the Rodgers specifically because Hamilton (and any show using vertical staging on this house's second-level balcony set piece) loses elevated action here — TickPick: 'the overhang from the Mezzanine can obstruct the viewing of that action if you are in the last rows.' Fodor's jv827: 'rear orchestra seats are situated below the overhang, blocking the top of the set in a few scenes.' Paying mid-tier for a seat where you duck is the wrong trade — go Rear Mezz Row A at half the price.

The eight boxes are a Krapp quirk — three movable chairs per box, closest you can get to stage without the front row. The Richard-Rodgers-specific tradeoff: AVFMS Box B reviewer GVseatview: 'Only missing the far left hand side of the stage (stage right). Excellent view. Comfortable seat with plenty of leg room' — i.e. you get the theatre's best legroom (rare here) but lose a specific corner of stage right. Lower boxes (A-D) sit closer to stage level than upper boxes (E-H) and angle better per TickPick/SeatPlan. Because seats are movable, the seat furthest from the stage in each box minimizes the angle loss.
